prize_parts.citation: for a poetry that has remade the Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and a critical, sustained dialogue with the inherited tradition

statement.case_for: My opening view still holds after reading colleagues' openings. Adonis offers the clearest combination of a distinctive voice, formal and linguistic achievement, and intellectual depth. Public knowledge of Songs of Mihyar the Damascene and A Time Between Ashes and Roses points to poetry that does more than add themes to Arabic verse. It reworks the language of the poem through myth and fragmentation while arguing with the tradition it inherits. The critical writing on that tradition belongs to the same project and is not an add-on. The oeuvre is fully formed over many decades, so timing is not a literary constraint. The significance is not only historical. The work poses the question of how a poetic language can renew itself from within its own inheritance. This is a question I take seriously as a reader of modern poetry, the fragment and the literature of displacement. I treat that scholarly interest as context, not as evidence that Adonis is the strongest candidate. The case has to rest on the poems, and on that basis I still find it the strongest in this field. Cărtărescu and Carson are close, and I would not be surprised if colleagues' arguments move the committee toward either.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that my judgement of Adonis depends on translation. Arabic prosody, sound and allusion carry over only partly, and I cannot independently verify the formal mastery that is the core of the claim. Several colleagues, Palm and Sward among them, have also pointed out that it is hard to separate the historical influence of a modernizer from the continuing force of the poems. I cannot yet show that the later collections sustain the level of the early and middle work. If the committee cannot establish that, the case rests more on influence than on achievement, and a candidate whose strength is more fully accessible in translation, such as Cărtărescu, would be the sounder choice. A related risk is that his public and critical positions could colour a reading of the whole body of work. They must not count for or against him.

responses.point: Palm ranks Adonis seventh. She acknowledges his very high historical significance for Arabic poetry. She asks whether durability should be judged by historical influence or also by the continuing force of the poems, and she warns that fame and public attention are not literary evidence.
responses.response: I accept the distinction and the warning about fame. The question about durability is the right one, and it is the one I cannot fully settle. My answer is that the argument should be tested on the poems themselves. Songs of Mihyar is not only a document of a turning point. Its fragmentary, mythic language still makes demands on the reader. I concede that I cannot show the same force across the later collections, and I would want the Academy's specialist reports on Arabic poetry to address that directly. Your case for Carson makes a different claim, that scholarship and poetry can be one practice. I find it persuasive as a claim about form, but it rests on a body of work that is more fragmentary in shape and whose relation to translation and scholarship is still open. That is why Carson stays an alternative for me and not my first choice.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Adonis sixth. She says Arabic prosody and linguistic experiment are hard to evaluate in translation and that his critical essays involve contested positions that could affect how the whole body of work is read. She cannot judge the weight of his later output.
responses.response: I share the translation concern and cannot dismiss it. It is the main uncertainty in my own case. I would qualify the second point. Contested positions in the essays should not lower the literary assessment, and they should not raise it either. The citation should rest on the poetry and on the essays only as far as they bear on poetic language. I agree that the later output is the real unknown. Your own first choice, Carson, shares part of the same difficulty. Her best-known work, Nox, depends on its physical form, and that does not reproduce in every medium. Neither of us is judging from a fully secure position. I would argue that the Arabic case calls for specialist input where Carson's calls for caution about format.

responses.point: Mattson puts Cărtărescu first for a highly recognizable visionary voice and an architecture of memory and body that extends across volumes. She ranks Adonis fourth and notes that his age makes timing a consideration, and that his literary significance is hard to separate from cultural or political positioning.
responses.response: I agree with your last point. Age and positioning are not literary criteria, and I would not let timing support Adonis, so I put them aside in my own assessment. Your argument for Cărtărescu is strong, and I moved him to my third place in my opening for much the same reasons. The difference between us is the translation question, which runs in both directions. You say his dense, rhythmic Romanian may not survive translation, and I agree. That is the same uncertainty that limits my confidence about Adonis. It is not a reason to rank one above the other. The deciding question is which body of work shows the more securely established achievement in its own language. I hold that the case for Adonis is the clearer one, but I recognize that it is a close judgement, and I keep Cărtărescu as my first alternative.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Adonis second behind Cărtărescu. He finds a long-term remaking of Arabic poetic language with intellectual depth in the essays, and he advises keeping political commentary separate from the literary assessment. He says he cannot judge formal mastery independently of the original.
responses.response: I agree that political commentary should be kept apart from the literary case. I share your uncertainty about formal mastery in translation. We differ only slightly in what follows from it. You put Cărtărescu first, and I understand why, since you describe the prose project as sustained and coherent over decades. If the committee concludes that the formal achievement in Arabic cannot be verified well enough, I would accept that this weakens my first choice and strengthens yours. I would not want the uncertainty to decide the matter by itself, because that would favour the writers who translate most readily. Whether the Academy's regional experts can close that gap is the point on which I think our two positions turn.

uncertainties: Whether translations of Adonis convey the prosody, sound and allusion that carry the formal achievement, and whether the later collections sustain the level of the early and middle work.
How to weigh the critical essays against the poems in a citation for the whole oeuvre, and how to keep contested public positions out of the literary assessment.
Whether the Academy's anonymous regional expert input on Arabic poetry is sufficient to settle the formal claims that translation cannot.
How far Cărtărescu's dense Romanian prose survives translation, and whether the largest novels sustain their intensity.
How to weigh Carson's hybrid, partly object-based works, and her translations and scholarship, against more conventional bodies of work under common criteria.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My scholarly interests in modern poetry, the fragment and exile literature are intellectual context only and are not treated as evidence of a preference for any candidate. No personal or institutional tie to the shortlisted writers appears in the profile.
